claims.text: The starting catalyst is a multi-element, nearly equiatomic automotive alloy catalyst.
The untreated alloy catalyst is prone to activity loss associated with sintering and oxidation under transient exhaust operation, H2O and NO exposure, and thermal aging.
An ultrathin CeO2 coating can be applied to the catalyst surface by atomic layer deposition.
The proposed CeO2 coating thickness ranges from sub-nanometer dimensions to a few nanometers.
ALD treatment will produce a well-adhered, uniform, conformal CeO2 nanolayer that forms a stable interface with the alloy.
The CeO2 nanolayer will mitigate surface sintering.
The CeO2 nanolayer will suppress uncontrolled oxidation of the alloy catalyst.
The CeO2 coating will act as an oxygen buffer and facilitate oxygen storage and release.
Oxygen storage and release by CeO2 will maintain favorable oxidation states at the catalyst surface.
The coating-mediated stabilization of surface oxidation states will protect the catalyst against sintering and phase degradation during thermal aging and transient operation.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, the CeO2-coated catalyst will retain higher pollutant-conversion activity after aging.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, the CeO2-coated catalyst will exhibit less activity degradation over aging cycles.
The durability improvement will not require additional platinum-group metals and will therefore preserve low platinum-group-metal consumption.
The proposed benefit is expected at approximately 200–300 °C under transient operation involving H2O, NO, and thermal cycling representative of gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust.
The magnitude and longevity of the improvement may vary with coating uniformity, interface stability, and interactions between the alloy and CeO2.
